📌 Address Poisoning: Why Your Transaction History Can Lie

Main Points
⏺ Scammers plant look-alike addresses in your wallet history
⏺ One careless copy-paste sends your funds to them
⏺ This post explains how the trick works and how to avoid it



1️⃣ Core Idea — Attackers create an address that starts and ends with the same characters as one you use, then send you a tiny or zero-value transfer from it so it shows up in your history.
2️⃣ Why It Happens — Most people check only the first and last few characters, and many wallets shorten addresses on screen. Copying "the last address I used" from history is a habit scammers count on.
3️⃣ Example — You regularly send USDT to your exchange. A dust transfer arrives from an address that looks the same at a glance; next time you copy from history and pick the fake one.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — Stablecoin transfers, wallets that display shortened addresses, and any payment you copy from recent activity instead of a saved contact.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — Never copy addresses from your transaction history. Use a saved address book, check the full address, and send a small test transfer before a large one.
Final Thoughts

Address poisoning doesn't hack your wallet — it hacks your attention. A few extra seconds of checking is the whole defense.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $582 million in net outflows on Thursday, November 19 — their third consecutive day of redemptions — as Bitcoin slipped below $62,000.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541 million of that figure, marking its largest single-day outflow on record. For the week, Bitcoin ETFs shed a combined $1.12 billion, with BlackRock responsible for $899 million of the total. Ether ETFs added $131 million in outflows on the same day, pushing combined BTC and ETH redemptions above $713 million for Thursday alone.

The week's outflow streak marks one of the sharpest stretches of institutional selling since U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs launched in January 2024.

When the Government Becomes the President's Advertising Agency 📢


A $20 million federal advertising campaign has raised a question that goes far beyond political messaging: where does the American government end and the president's personal political brand begin?

The controversy centers on advertisements funded through a Department of Homeland Security contract and featuring Trump. 

Some included footage previously used in his 2024 presidential campaign, alongside messages promoting his administration's policies.

The White House defended the campaign as public information. Critics, including government accountability organizations, argued that taxpayer money was being used to amplify the president's political image ahead of the November midterm elections.

The legal battle has produced competing developments. On October 28, a federal judge in Washington temporarily blocked the use of $20 million in federal funds for the challenged advertisements. On November 20, however, a separate judge in New York declined to impose a longer-term ban, reasoning that the immediate electoral circumstances had changed after Election Day. The Washington litigation remains ongoing.

The deeper issue is institutional rather than financial. Government advertising is supposed to serve the public, not the political interests of whoever occupies the Oval Office. When presidential imagery, campaign material and official communications begin to overlap, citizens have fewer ways to distinguish public information from political persuasion.

The most troubling possibility is not that a president might advertise himself with public money. It is that such practices could gradually become normal, making the distinction between the state and the political leader seem increasingly irrelevant.

Democracy depends not only on free elections, but also on a government that does not confuse its own interests with those of the country.

🦅 THE GOLD COIN THAT SOLD FOR $9.36 MILLION

In 1787, before the United States had a national mint, New York gold and silversmith Ephraim Brasher struck a small number of gold coins of his own.

His New York-style design shows a sun rising over a mountain, much like the New York state seal, with an eagle on the other side. Brasher punched his initials, "EB," into each coin.

Brasher doubloons are among the first gold coins struck in the newly independent United States. Only nine are known, seven of them in the New York style.

On January 21, 2021, the finest known example, with the EB on the eagle's wing, sold at Heritage Auctions for $9.36 million, then the highest price ever paid for a gold coin at auction.
